These notes explore ideas from my MATH1972 seminars at the University of Sydney. They cover game theory, optimisation, machine learning, and networks.

Each note develops the ideas behind the definitions. Short proofs explain why the main results work. Small examples show how to use them. The notes draw on seminar material. The figures and worked numerical examples were created for these notes. External references are listed where they help explain an idea.

## Game Theory

[**Nim and Winning Moves**](nim.qmd)

Start with a game of stones. Learn why some positions let you force a win. Build the XOR rule from simple cases, then use it to find winning moves.

## Optimisation and Machine Learning

Read these four notes in order if the topic is new to you.

1. [**Convex Sets and Functions**](convexity.qmd) — understand the geometry that makes optimisation easier. See why a local minimum is also global.
2. [**Lagrange Duality and KKT Conditions**](duality-kkt.qmd) — turn constraints into useful bounds. Work through active and inactive constraints.
3. [**Linear SVMs and Margins**](linear-svm.qmd) — connect a geometric gap with a quadratic programme. Follow the primal and dual derivations.
4. [**Feature Maps and Kernels**](kernels.qmd) — use richer features through inner products. Check a small feature map by hand.

For a related application, see the [Multiclass SVM project](../../projects/multiclass-svm-crammer-singer.qmd). It extends the margin idea to several classes.

## Network Analysis

[**Introduction to Network Analysis**](network-analysis.qmd)

Use one seven-node graph to explore degree, density, clustering, and distance. Learn what each measure tells us and what it leaves out.

[**Random Networks and Connectivity**](random-networks.qmd)

Build a graph from independent random edges. Derive degree and edge-count distributions, then use expectation and variance to study isolated nodes and connectivity. See why short typical routes do not imply that the whole graph is connected.
